---
title: "What goes with school absence"
subtitle: "A first look at the causes of school-level absence in England's secondary schools, framed by the research and tested on published data for every school."
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "site_helpers.R"))
A <- readRDS(here::here("data", "absence_causes.rds"))
OUT <- A$outcomes
OUT_SHORT <- c(overall = "Overall", illness = "Illness", appointments = "Medical\nappointments",
               auth_other = "Other\nauthorised", unauth = "Unauthorised", persistent = "Persistent\n(10%+)",
               severe = "Severe\n(50%+)")
TERM_LAB <- c(A$cont,
  sixthTRUE = "Has a sixth form (vs 11-16)",
  ADMPOL_PTSEL = "Selective (vs non-selective, selective area)",
  `ADMPOL_PTOTHER NON SEL` = "Non-selective elsewhere (vs same)",
  `matMulti-academy trust` = "Multi-academy trust (vs maintained)",
  `matSingle-academy trust or not recorded` = "Single-academy trust (vs maintained)",
  faithTRUE = "Religious character (vs none)",
  `placeUrban, further from one` = "Urban, further from a city (vs nearer)",
  placeRural = "Rural (vs urban, nearer a city)")
TERM_GROUP <- c(fsm = "Poverty", sen_sup = "SEND", ehcp = "SEND", semh = "SEND", asd = "SEND", learning = "SEND",
  carer = "Young carers", eal = "Ethnicity and language", wbri = "Ethnicity and language",
  grt = "Ethnicity and language", ks2_c = "Prior attainment and neighbourhood",
  z_l4 = "Prior attainment and neighbourhood", mobile = "Mobility and sex", girls = "Mobility and sex",
  size = "The school", sixthTRUE = "The school", ADMPOL_PTSEL = "The school",
  `ADMPOL_PTOTHER NON SEL` = "The school", `matMulti-academy trust` = "The school",
  `matSingle-academy trust or not recorded` = "The school", faithTRUE = "The school",
  `placeUrban, further from one` = "Place", placeRural = "Place")
e <- function(term, out) A$effects$pct[A$effects$term == term & A$effects$outcome == out]
sg <- function(x, d = 0) sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f%%"), x)
tr <- function(yr, col) A$trend[[col]][A$trend$year == yr]
part <- function(out, col) A$partition[[col]][A$partition$outcome == out]
r2 <- function(out) A$shapley$r2_full[A$shapley$outcome == out][1]
la_rank <- A$la_effects |> group_by(outcome) |>
  mutate(rank = rank(-la_pct), n = n()) |> ungroup()
bh <- function(out, col) la_rank[[col]][la_rank$outcome == out & la_rank$la == "Brighton and Hove"]
n_la <- max(la_rank$n)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Work in progress

This is the first cut of the absence analysis on the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd).
It describes how absence varies between schools, and with what. It does not
yet say why. Every figure comes from published school-level data, so every
result is an association between schools, not an effect on pupils.
:::

## Why this matters for value added

Absence is the largest single term in Value Added v2.1's expectation. The
model takes each school's absence as given: a school with more absence is
expected to get lower results. That is fair to schools whose absence is
outside their control. It is unfair if some of that absence is something
the school could have prevented. To tell the two apart, we need to know
what absence goes with. This page makes a start.

## What the research says {#sec-research}

A research map of UK work since 2016 (summarised below; sources at the
foot of the page) says absence is not one behaviour with one cause. Health,
family, peer, school and wider circumstances all bear on it, and they
interact. It is higher in secondary schools, rises with age, and is
concentrated among pupils facing poverty, special educational needs,
health difficulties and other disadvantage. Absence harms attainment
whether or not it is authorised, but it is also a marker of difficulties
that were already there.

The post-pandemic rise is real and not fully explained. The leading
accounts are:

- more illness;
- anxiety and avoiding school;
- broken routines and weaker attendance norms;
- unmet SEND needs;
- strained relations between home and school;
- slow access to support.

No single cause has been shown to dominate.

Each strand of that research suggests something we can measure for every
school in England:

| The research points to | What we can measure for each school | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Physical illness, the most common recorded reason | Illness as a share of possible sessions, as its own outcome | DfE absence data |
| Mental health, anxiety, school-related distress | Pupils whose main SEN need is social, emotional and mental health | DfE SEN data, January 2026 |
| SEND, and gaps that have not closed | SEN support, EHC plans, autism, learning difficulties | DfE SEN data |
| Poverty and family circumstances | Free school meals; young carers | School census, January 2026 |
| Differences by ethnicity and sex | White British, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller, EAL; share of girls | School census |
| Prior attainment and disengagement | KS2 prior attainment; neighbourhood education | Value Added inputs |
| School experience: climate, belonging, fit | Only proxies: size, sixth form, admissions, governance, faith | Census, GIAS |
| Place | Region, local authority, rural or urban | Census |
| Post-COVID norms | The trend by reason; not testable across schools in one year | DfE absence data |

Ofsted grades are left out on purpose. Attendance is part of what an
inspection judges, so a grade would partly be absence measured again.

## How absence has changed, by reason {#sec-trend}

```{r}
#| label: fig-trend
#| fig-cap: "Absence by reason in England's state-funded secondary schools, % of possible sessions, full years, 2016/17 to 2024/25 (sessions-weighted; DfE school-level absence data). 2019/20 was not collected; 2020/21 was a year of partial closure."
#| fig-height: 4.6
tr_long <- A$trend |> select(-persistent, -severe) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(year = "2019/20")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "reason", values_to = "rate") |>
  filter(!is.na(reason)) |>
  mutate(x = as.integer(substr(year, 1, 4)),
         reason = factor(reason, c("Illness", "Other unauthorised", "Other authorised",
                                   "Medical appointments", "Unauthorised holiday")))
ggplot(tr_long, aes(x, rate, colour = reason)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2019.5, xmax = 2020.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = PPURPLE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) + geom_point(size = 1.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(data = tr_long |> filter(x == 2024) |>
              mutate(rate = rate + case_when(reason == "Medical appointments" ~ 0.12,
                                             reason == "Unauthorised holiday" ~ -0.1, TRUE ~ 0)),
            aes(label = reason), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.15, size = 3.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(DPURPLE, BLUE, BPURPLE, GREY, MPURPLE), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2016:2024, labels = function(x) paste0(x, "/", substr(x + 1, 3, 4)),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.32))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of possible sessions") + theme_note()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trend-pa
#| fig-cap: "Persistent absence (missing 10% or more of sessions) and severe absence (50% or more), % of pupils, same schools and years."
#| fig-height: 3.4
pa <- A$trend |> select(year, `Persistent (10%+)` = persistent, `Severe (50%+)` = severe) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(year = "2019/20")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate") |> filter(!is.na(measure)) |>
  mutate(x = as.integer(substr(year, 1, 4)))
ggplot(pa, aes(x, rate)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2019.5, xmax = 2020.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = PPURPLE) +
  geom_line(colour = DPURPLE, linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) + geom_point(colour = DPURPLE, size = 1.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "/", substr(x + 1, 3, 4))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of pupils") + theme_note()
```

The reasons have not moved together:

- **Illness** jumped from `r pp(tr("2018/19", "Illness"))`% of sessions
  in 2018/19 to `r pp(tr("2021/22", "Illness"))`% in 2021/22. By 2024/25
  it had fallen back to `r pp(tr("2024/25", "Illness"))`%, most of the
  way home.
- **Unauthorised absence other than holidays** doubled, from
  `r pp(tr("2018/19", "Other unauthorised"))`% to
  `r pp(tr("2023/24", "Other unauthorised"))`% in 2023/24. It has barely
  come down since.
- **Severe absence** rose every year, from `r pp(tr("2018/19", "severe"))`%
  of pupils to `r pp(tr("2024/25", "severe"))`%, nearly three times as many.

Persistent absence is falling, but the tail is still growing. That matches
the research: the average can improve while the worst cases get worse.

## What goes with absence, school by school {#sec-effects}

The model covers `r format(A$n_schools, big.mark = ",")` state-funded
secondary schools with full data. It uses their absence in the autumn and
spring terms of 2025/26 and their intake as recorded in the January 2026
school census and SEN data. For each of seven outcomes, it is a multilevel
model of the outcome (logged) on all the characteristics at once, with
region and local authority effects.

Each number below is the difference in that kind of absence that goes with
one standard deviation more of a characteristic, all else equal. A
standard deviation is roughly the gap between a typical school and one
noticeably above it. For yes-or-no characteristics, the number compares
the two kinds of school. Purple means more absence, green less. Blank
cells are differences that could be zero.

```{r}
#| label: fig-effects
#| fig-cap: "Difference in each kind of absence (%) with one standard deviation more of each characteristic (yes vs no for the categories), all else equal: multilevel models with region and local authority effects, 2025/26 autumn and spring terms. Purple, more absence; green, less. Blank, the 95% interval includes zero."
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig-width: 9
ef <- A$effects |>
  mutate(label = unname(TERM_LAB[term]), grp = unname(TERM_GROUP[term]),
         sig = lo > 0 | hi < 0,
         out = factor(OUT_SHORT[outcome], OUT_SHORT),
         grp = factor(grp, names(A$groups)),
         fillv = ifelse(sig, pmax(pmin(pct, 30), -30), NA))
lev <- ef |> distinct(term, label, grp) |> arrange(grp, match(term, unique(ef$term))) |> pull(label)
ef$label <- factor(ef$label, rev(lev))
ggplot(ef, aes(out, label)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = fillv), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.0f", pct), colour = ifelse(!sig, "ns", ifelse(abs(pct) > 18, "dark", "sig"))), size = 3.6) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#1b7837", "#5aae61", "#d9f0d3", "#f7f7f7", "#e7d4e8", "#9970ab", "#762a83"),
                       limits = c(-30, 30), na.value = "white", name = "% difference",
                       labels = function(x) ifelse(abs(x) == 30, paste0(ifelse(x > 0, "≥ +", "≤ "), x), sprintf("%+d", x))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(sig = INK, dark = "white", ns = "#a8a3b8"), guide = "none") +
  facet_grid(grp ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_note(12) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1, size = 9),
        legend.key.width = unit(1.6, "cm"))
```

What stands out:

- **Poverty, prior attainment and mobility go with the absence a school has
  least claim to.** With one SD more pupils on free school meals,
  unauthorised absence is `r sg(e("fsm", "unauth"))` and severe absence
  `r sg(e("fsm", "severe"))`. Illness, once everything else is allowed
  for, is `r sg(e("fsm", "illness"))`. Lower KS2 prior attainment and more
  pupils joining mid-phase point the same way.
- **Among the types of need, social, emotional and mental health need is
  the one that matters.** One SD more of it goes with
  `r sg(e("semh", "severe"))` severe and `r sg(e("semh", "auth_other"))`
  other authorised absence. Once the types of need are in the model, the
  share of pupils on SEN support or with EHC plans adds nothing more. This
  fits the research's emphasis on anxiety and distress.
- **Schools with more White British pupils have more absence of every
  kind**, especially severe (`r sg(e("wbri", "severe"))` per SD) and
  unauthorised (`r sg(e("wbri", "unauth"))`). EAL goes the other way. This
  is a comparison between schools, not pupils. It matches the national
  statistics, where absence is lower among most minority ethnic groups. It
  does not say why.
- **Girls.** Schools with more girls have more medical-appointment
  (`r sg(e("girls", "appointments"))`) and severe absence
  (`r sg(e("girls", "severe"))`). This matches the research finding that
  girls are absent more than boys.
- **The school.**
  - Selective schools have far less unauthorised
    (`r sg(e("ADMPOL_PTSEL", "unauth"))`) and severe absence
    (`r sg(e("ADMPOL_PTSEL", "severe"))`) than intake alone predicts.
  - Schools with a religious character have somewhat less
    (`r sg(e("faithTRUE", "unauth"))` unauthorised).
  - Schools with a sixth form have *more* absence among their 11-16 pupils
    (`r sg(e("sixthTRUE", "overall"))` overall). This echoes Value Added
    v2.1, where 11-16 schools do better.
  - Being in a multi-academy trust makes little difference.
- **Place.** Rural schools record `r sg(e("placeRural", "appointments"))`
  absence for medical appointments and `r sg(e("placeRural", "unauth"))`
  unauthorised absence, against urban schools near a city. A plausible reading is that getting to an
  appointment from a rural school costs a whole session rather than part of
  one. That bears on the [distance-to-school](roadmap.qmd) question.
- **Young carers barely register.** This is more likely a measurement
  problem than a finding: schools differ widely in how many young carers
  they identify.

## How much each group explains {#sec-shapley}

```{r}
#| label: fig-shapley
#| fig-cap: "Share of the variation between schools in each kind of absence (logged) explained by each group of characteristics: Shapley values of R² from OLS, region in Place. Each column sums to the total R² shown at the foot."
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 9
sh <- A$shapley |> mutate(out = factor(OUT_SHORT[outcome], OUT_SHORT),
                          group = factor(group, rev(names(A$groups))))
tot <- sh |> distinct(out, r2_full) |> mutate(group = "Total R²")
ggplot(sh, aes(out, group)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = 100 * shapley), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * shapley), colour = shapley > 0.11), size = 3.7) +
  geom_tile(data = tot, aes(out, group), fill = "white", colour = LIGHT) +
  geom_text(data = tot, aes(out, group, label = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r2_full)), fontface = "bold",
            colour = DPURPLE, size = 3.8) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = c("Total R²", levels(sh$group))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = PPURPLE, high = DPURPLE, name = "Percentage points of R²") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = INK), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_note(12) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.key.width = unit(1.6, "cm"))
```

The kinds of absence split cleanly in two:

- **Unauthorised, persistent and severe absence are mostly about who the
  pupils are.** Intake and school characteristics account for between
  `r round(100 * min(r2("severe"), r2("persistent"), r2("unauth")))`% and
  `r round(100 * max(r2("severe"), r2("persistent"), r2("unauth")))`% of
  the variation. Poverty, prior attainment and the school itself carry most
  of it.
- **Illness and medical appointments are mostly not.** Only
  `r round(100 * r2("illness"))`% and `r round(100 * r2("appointments"))`%
  is accounted for, and Place is the largest single group for both. Two
  schools with the same intake can record very different amounts of
  illness.

That is the case for v2.1's sensitivity test that counts illness separately
from other absence ([Methodology](method.qmd#sec-v21)).

## The school's part {#sec-school}

"The school" carries `r round(100 * A$shapley$shapley[A$shapley$outcome == "unauth" & A$shapley$group == "The school"])`
to `r round(100 * A$shapley$shapley[A$shapley$outcome == "persistent" & A$shapley$group == "The school"])`
points of R² for unauthorised, persistent and severe absence above. That
does not mean schools are to blame for that much absence. The group is five
measured features:

- size;
- whether the school has a sixth form;
- its admissions (selective, or non-selective);
- who runs it;
- whether it has a religious character.

What schools *do* is not measured at all. Splitting the group into its
five features shows where the credit goes:

```{r}
#| label: fig-school-split
#| fig-cap: "The school group's share of R², split into its five features: Shapley values with each feature as a player of its own and the other seven groups as before (OLS, region in Place), 2025/26 autumn and spring."
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 9
SCHOOL_LAB <- c(ADMPOL_PT = "Admissions (selective or not)", mat = "Who runs it", size = "Size",
                sixth = "Sixth form", faith = "Religious character")
ss <- A$shap_school |> filter(player %in% names(SCHOOL_LAB)) |>
  mutate(player = factor(SCHOOL_LAB[player], rev(SCHOOL_LAB)), out = factor(OUT_SHORT[outcome], OUT_SHORT))
ggplot(ss, aes(100 * shapley, player)) +
  geom_col(fill = DPURPLE, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * shapley)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = INK) +
  facet_wrap(~ out, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  labs(x = "Percentage points of R²", y = NULL) + theme_note() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
sc <- function(o, p) 100 * A$shap_school$shapley[A$shap_school$outcome == o & A$shap_school$player == p]
sp <- function(o, col) A$school_spread[[col]][A$school_spread$outcome == o]
```

**Most of it is selection.** Admissions accounts for
`r pp(sc("unauth", "ADMPOL_PT"))` of the points for unauthorised absence,
`r pp(sc("persistent", "ADMPOL_PT"))` for persistent and
`r pp(sc("severe", "ADMPOL_PT"))` for severe. Selective schools choose
their pupils. Prior attainment and free school meals measure some of what
selection does, but not all of it, and admissions picks up the rest. That
is a fact about who comes to the school, not about how it is run. Who runs
it (`r pp(sc("unauth", "mat"))` points), size, sixth form and religious
character each add little.

**What a school does shows up somewhere else: in how far apart similar
schools are.** Take schools with the same intake, needs and setting, in the
same local authority. What is left over (the models' school-level
residuals) is what the measured characteristics cannot explain. That
includes how a school runs attendance, and also anything about its pupils
the data does not see.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-school-spread
#| tbl-cap: "How far apart schools with the same intake, needs and setting, in the same local authority, are on each kind of absence (2025/26 autumn and spring), and whether the differences repeat (the same models on 2024/25 full-year absence)."
A$school_spread |> mutate(o = factor(outcome, names(OUT))) |> arrange(o) |>
  transmute(Outcome = unname(OUT[outcome]),
            `Quarter from top vs quarter from bottom` = sprintf("%+.0f%%", iqr_pct),
            `Tenth from top vs tenth from bottom` = sprintf("%+.0f%%", p90_10_pct),
            `Correlation with 2024/25` = sprintf("%.2f", r_years),
            `Top quarter in 2025/26 also top quarter in 2024/25` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * top_q_again)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

- **The gaps are large.** Among otherwise similar schools in the same
  authority, the one a quarter of the way from the top has
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", sp("unauth", "iqr_pct"))` more unauthorised absence
  than the one a quarter of the way from the bottom. For severe absence the
  gap is `r sprintf("%.0f%%", sp("severe", "iqr_pct"))`; for overall
  absence, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", sp("overall", "iqr_pct"))`.
- **They repeat.** A school's unexplained absence in 2025/26 correlates
  `r sprintf("%.2f", sp("unauth", "r_years"))` with its own in 2024/25 for
  unauthorised absence, and `r sprintf("%.2f", sp("overall", "r_years"))`
  overall. Of the schools in the top quarter for unexplained unauthorised
  absence in 2025/26, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sp("unauth", "top_q_again"))`
  were in the top quarter the year before; chance would give 25%. These are
  stable features of schools or their communities, not noise.
- **That stability is not proof of a school effect.** The same 2026
  characteristics are used for both years, and pupils the data does not see
  are as stable as a school's practice. Only following schools whose
  practice changed would separate the two.

::: {.callout-tip}
## For heads and governors

1. **Judge absence against what your intake predicts, not against the
   national average.** The area pages give each Sussex school's absence by
   kind, its prediction, and how it compares with similar schools in the
   same authority over two years.
2. **Structure is not the lever.** Being in a multi-academy trust, its
   size, and its religious character make little difference once intake is
   allowed for. Most of what looks like a "school" effect in the averages is
   selective admissions, which is about who is admitted.
3. **Practice may well be the lever.** Schools with the same intake differ
   by half again or more in unauthorised and severe absence, and the
   differences persist. A school well above similar schools, year after
   year, should ask what its look-alikes below the line are doing
   differently.
4. **Look at the kind of absence.** Unauthorised, persistent and severe
   absence are where similar schools differ most. Illness differs mostly by
   place, and partly by how readily it is authorised.
5. **The research points to where to look.** It is consistent on:
   - early identification;
   - relationships and belonging;
   - support for social, emotional and mental health needs (the type of
     need that goes most with absence here);
   - work with families. Parental engagement is the one approach with
     consistent support from randomised trials, though most were in the
     United States.
6. **Schools with a sixth form** have `r sg(e("sixthTRUE", "overall"))`
   more absence among their 11-16 pupils than comparable 11-16 schools.
   That is worth a look in 11-18 schools.
:::

## Place, once the intake is allowed for {#sec-place}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-place
#| tbl-cap: "Share of the variation between schools at the region and local authority levels, before and after the characteristics are in the model (multilevel models, 2025/26 autumn and spring)."
A$partition |>
  transmute(Outcome = unname(OUT[outcome]),
            `Region and authority, before` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (la_null + region_null)),
            `Region and authority, after` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (la_full + region_full)),
            `Explained by the characteristics` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r2_fixed)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

For most kinds of absence, a school's region and authority matter little
once its intake is known. Illness and other authorised absence are the
exceptions: about
`r round(100 * (part("illness", "la_full") + part("illness", "region_full")))`% and
`r round(100 * (part("auth_other", "la_full") + part("auth_other", "region_full")))`%
of the variation between schools is still at the region and authority
levels after allowing for intake. Both are kinds of absence a school chooses
to authorise. Some places' schools record more illness
than their intakes predict. That could be because their pupils really are
ill more often. It could also be because schools in those places authorise
absence as illness more readily, so that the same absence elsewhere would
be recorded as unauthorised. The data cannot tell these apart.

```{r}
#| label: fig-la-illness
#| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Each local authority's illness absence against what its schools' intakes predict, 2025/26 autumn and spring (multilevel model, region and authority effects together). ", n_la, " authorities, lowest on the left; Sussex's three are named.")
#| fig-height: 4.2
li <- la_rank |> filter(outcome == "illness") |> arrange(la_pct) |>
  mutate(pos = row_number(), sussex = la %in% c("Brighton and Hove", "East Sussex", "West Sussex"))
ggplot(li, aes(pos, la_pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = LIGHT) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = sussex), width = 0.85) +
  geom_text(data = li |> filter(sussex), aes(label = paste0(la, " ", sg(la_pct))),
            hjust = ifelse(li$la_pct[li$sussex] > 0, -0.08, 1.08), angle = 90, size = 3.2, colour = DPURPLE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = DPURPLE, `FALSE` = LIGHT), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) sprintf("%+d%%", x), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.9))) +
  labs(x = "Local authorities, lowest to highest", y = "Illness against intake") + theme_note() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

**Brighton and Hove** records `r sg(bh("illness", "la_pct"))` more illness
absence than its schools' intakes predict, the
`r ord(bh("illness", "rank"))` highest of `r n_la` authorities. Its
unauthorised absence is `r sg(bh("unauth", "la_pct"))` against intake
(`r ord(bh("unauth", "rank"))`). The city's high absence, which the
[Geographical effects](bh_effect.qmd) page finds costs its pupils so little
attainment, is illness absence, and its intake does not explain it. That
fits both readings above: an unusual amount of illness, or a habit of
authorising absence as illness that elsewhere would go unauthorised. Which
it is matters for value added. If it is recording, the city's absence is
not the kind that costs attainment, and the model's absence term
over-forgives it.

## The full models {#sec-full}

Each of the seven outcomes has the same multilevel model. For school $i$ in
local authority $j$ in region $k$:

$$\log(y_{ijk} + 0.1) = \beta_0 + \sum_p \beta_p\, x_{p,ijk} + u_k + v_{jk} + e_{ijk}$$

$$u_k \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{region}}), \quad v_{jk} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{LA}}), \quad e_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{school}})$$

- **The outcome** $y$ is a percentage: of possible sessions for the five
  kinds of absence, of pupils for persistent and severe. The 0.1 lets
  severe absence be zero.
- **The measured characteristics** $x$ are standardised to mean 0 and SD 1,
  so each $\beta$ is the change in log absence for one SD, and
  $100\,(e^{\beta} - 1)$ is the % difference shown in @fig-effects.
- **The categories** are compared with a reference: 11-16, non-selective
  in a selective area, maintained, no religious character, and urban near a
  major town or city.
- **Estimation** is REML in `lme4`. The log-likelihoods, AIC and BIC are
  from the same models refitted by maximum likelihood. The marginal R² is
  the variance of the fixed-effect predictions over the total; the
  conditional R² adds the region and authority effects (Nakagawa and
  Schielzeth). "Explained by the characteristics" is the fall in total
  variance from the model with no characteristics.

```{r}
#| label: model-helpers
#| include: false
OUT_FLAT <- gsub("\n", " ", OUT_SHORT)
fixed_tbl <- function(o) {
  A$coefs |> filter(outcome == o) |>
    mutate(Term = ifelse(term == "(Intercept)", "Intercept (reference school, mean characteristics)",
                         unname(TERM_LAB[term])),
           Estimate = sprintf("%.3f", b), SE = sprintf("%.3f", se), t = sprintf("%.1f", t),
           `% difference (95% CI)` = ifelse(term == "(Intercept)", "",
             sprintf("%+.1f (%+.1f to %+.1f)", 100 * (exp(b) - 1), 100 * (exp(b - 1.96 * se) - 1),
                     100 * (exp(b + 1.96 * se) - 1)))) |>
    select(Term, Estimate, SE, t, `% difference (95% CI)`)
}
re_tbl <- function(o) {
  A$random |> filter(outcome == o) |>
    mutate(tot0 = sum(var_null)) |>
    transmute(Level = level, `Variance, no characteristics` = sprintf("%.4f", var_null),
              `Variance, full model` = sprintf("%.4f", var_full),
              `Share of the starting total, after` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * var_full / tot0))
}
fit_tbl <- function(o) {
  f <- A$fit |> filter(outcome == o); p <- A$partition |> filter(outcome == o)
  tibble(Measure = c("Schools", "Local authorities", "Regions", "Mean outcome (%)",
                     "Explained by the characteristics", "Marginal R² (fixed effects)",
                     "Conditional R² (with region and authority)", "OLS R² (Shapley total, region fixed)",
                     "Log-likelihood (ML)", "Log-likelihood, no characteristics (ML)", "AIC", "BIC"),
         Value = c(format(f$n_school, big.mark = ","), f$n_la, f$n_region, sprintf("%.2f", f$mean_y),
                   sprintf("%.3f", p$r2_fixed), sprintf("%.3f", f$r2_marginal), sprintf("%.3f", f$r2_conditional),
                   sprintf("%.3f", r2(o)), sprintf("%.1f", f$loglik), sprintf("%.1f", f$loglik_null),
                   sprintf("%.1f", f$aic), sprintf("%.1f", f$bic)))
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}
```{r}
#| label: full-model-tables
#| output: asis
for (o in names(OUT)) {
  cat("\n## ", OUT_FLAT[[o]], "\n\n", sep = "")
  cat(as.character(kt(fixed_tbl(o), align = "lrrrr",
    caption = paste0(OUT[[o]], ": fixed effects. Estimates are on the log scale, per SD for a measured characteristic, against the reference for a category."))), "\n\n")
  cat(as.character(kt(re_tbl(o), align = "lrrr",
    caption = "Random effects: the variance at each level, with no characteristics and in the full model.")), "\n\n")
  cat(as.character(kt(fit_tbl(o), align = "lr", caption = "Data and fit.")), "\n\n")
}
```
:::

What one standard deviation is, in each characteristic's own units, for
the `r format(A$n_schools, big.mark = ",")` schools in the models, and how
many schools fall in each category:

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Measured characteristics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-x-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Measured characteristics: mean and standard deviation across the schools in the models. KS2 prior attainment is centred and neighbourhood education is already a z-score; size is the log of pupils on roll."
A$x_desc |> transmute(Characteristic = unname(A$cont[var]), Mean = sprintf("%.2f", mean),
                      `One SD` = sprintf("%.2f", sd)) |> kt(align = "lrr")
```

## Categories

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cat-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Categories: schools in each, with the reference category first."
CAT_LAB <- c(sixth = "Sixth form", ADMPOL_PT = "Admissions", mat = "Governance", faith = "Religious character",
             place = "Rural or urban")
LEVEL_LAB <- c(`FALSE` = "No", `TRUE` = "Yes", `OTHER NON SEL` = "Non-selective elsewhere",
               SEL = "Selective", `NON SEL IN HIGHLY SEL AREA` = "Non-selective in a selective area")
A$cat_desc |> transmute(Characteristic = unname(CAT_LAB[var]),
                        Category = coalesce(unname(LEVEL_LAB[level]), level), Schools = n) |>
  kt(align = "llr")
```
:::

## What this cannot tell us {#sec-limits}

- **Schools, not pupils.** A school with more pupils on free school meals
  having more absence does not show that its pupils on free school meals
  are the ones absent.
- **Association, not cause.** Some of the school characteristics may follow
  from absence rather than lead to it, such as a school's size or who runs
  it.
- **Two terms of one year.** Autumn and spring carry more illness than
  summer, and one year is a snapshot. The trend figures are full years.
- **Measured needs only.** SEN data counts identified need. The research
  warns that unmet or unidentified need sits outside it, and so do young
  carers not known to their school.
- **School climate is unmeasured.** Belonging, bullying, relationships and
  fit come out of the research as important, and nothing here measures
  them.

## Next steps {#sec-next}

1. **Within-school change.** Follow schools from 2021/22 to 2025/26 to see
   whether absence moves when intake does. That is a stronger test than one
   year's snapshot.
2. **Illness or recording?** Look at how illness and unauthorised absence
   trade off within authorities, to see whether high-illness places are
   recording differently.
3. **Distance to school**, from the roadmap. The rural appointments result
   gives a first reason to expect it to matter.
4. **The severe tail.** Severe absence is rising while the average falls.
   It needs its own model.
5. **Back into value added.** Absence against intake, split by kind, could
   replace raw absence in a future version of the model.

The research summary draws on a
[research map of UK work since 2016](https://github.com/adamdennett/school_value_added/blob/main/Elicit%20-%20UK%20School%20Absence%20Research%20Map%2C%202016%E2%80%932026.md)
(compiled with Elicit), including:

- Department for Education (2025), [*Pupil absence in schools in England: autumn and spring term 2024/25*](https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/find-statistics/pupil-absence-in-schools-in-england/2024-25-autumn-and-spring-term).
- Hunt and Wielar (2025), [*Examining post-pandemic absences in England (5)*](https://epi.org.uk/publications-and-research/examining-post-pandemic-absences-in-england-5/), Education Policy Institute.
- Finning et al. (2019), [practitioners' beliefs about risk factors for attendance problems](https://doi.org/10.1080/13632752.2019.1647684), *Emotional and Behavioural Difficulties*.
- Lereya et al. (2022), [special educational need and absence over time and across need types](https://doi.org/10.1080/08856257.2022.2059631), *European Journal of Special Needs Education*.
- McDonald, Lester and Michelson (2022), [attendance problems in the context of COVID-19](https://sussex.figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/_She_didn_t_know_how_to_go_back_school_attendance_problems_in_the_context_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_-_a_multiple_stakeholder_qualitative_study_with_parents_and_professionals/23493092), *British Journal of Educational Psychology* (accepted manuscript).
- Klein, Dare and Sosu (2019), [socioeconomic inequalities in school absenteeism](https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/id/eprint/72714), European Conference on Educational Research paper.
- Anders et al. (2025), [the post-pandemic rise in teenage skipping across English-speaking countries](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-025-09470-z), *Educational Assessment, Evaluation and Accountability*.
- Dräger, Klein and Sosu (2025), [whether the timing of absence changes its effect on achievement](https://doi.org/10.3102/00028312251347666), *American Educational Research Journal*.
- Dräger, Klein and Sosu (2026), [absence as a mediator of the socioeconomic achievement gap](https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/97231/), *Research in Social Stratification and Mobility*.
- Epstein et al. (2026), [absence and later mental health in adolescents in England](https://doi.org/10.1111/camh.70113), *Child and Adolescent Mental Health*.
- Troncoso et al. (2026), [disadvantage, attendance and exclusions in Scotland](https://doi.org/10.23889/ijpds.v11i5.3529), *International Journal of Population Data Science*.
- Strelitz et al. (2026), [interventions to improve school attendance](https://doi.org/10.1136/jech-2025-225671), *Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health*.

Data: DfE school-level absence (2016/17 to 2024/25, full years; 2025/26,
autumn and spring), the January 2026 school census and SEN school-level
data, GIAS, and the Value Added v2.1 inputs. Code: `R/08_absence_causes.R`.
